content: In Bayesian probability theory, a prior probability distribution ( p(theta) ) is considered conjugate to a likelihood function ( p(x | theta) ) if the resulting posterior distribution ( p(theta | x) ) belongs to the same family of distributions as the prior ( p(theta) ). For instance, the Gaussian distribution is self-conjugate, meaning that if the likelihood function is Gaussian and the prior is also Gaussian, the posterior distribution will remain Gaussian. The concept of conjugate priors, as well as the term itself, was introduced by Howard Raiffa and Robert Schlaifer in their work on Bayesian decision theory. Independently, George Alfred Barnard also discovered a similar concept. To understand this, consider the general problem of inferring a distribution for a parameter ( theta ) based on observed data ( x ). According to Bayes' theorem, the posterior distribution is derived from the prior ( p(theta) ) and the likelihood function ( p(x | theta) ). The likelihood function is typically fixed and determined by the data-generating process. However, the choice of the prior distribution ( p(theta) ) can significantly affect the complexity of the calculations. Specifically, the product ( p(x | theta) times p(theta) ) may take on different algebraic forms depending on the prior chosen. For certain priors, the posterior distribution retains the same algebraic form as the prior, albeit with updated parameters. Such priors are referred to as conjugate priors. The use of a conjugate prior is often an algebraic convenience, as it avoids the need for complex numerical integration. Members of the exponential family of distributions all have conjugate priors, and detailed catalogs of these relationships can be found in works such as those by Gelman et al. As an example, consider a random variable following a Bernoulli distribution with an unknown probability of success ( q ). The usual conjugate prior for this scenario is the Beta distribution, parameterized by ( alpha ) and ( beta ), which reflect prior beliefs or information. For instance, setting ( alpha = 1 ) and ( beta = 1 ) results in a uniform distribution. The Beta function ( B(alpha, beta) ) serves as a normalizing constant. If we observe ( s ) successes and ( f ) failures from this Bernoulli process, the posterior distribution is another Beta distribution with updated parameters ( alpha + s ) and ( beta + f ). This posterior distribution can then be used as the prior for subsequent data, with the parameters being incrementally updated as new information becomes available. In summary, conjugate priors simplify Bayesian inference by ensuring that the posterior distribution remains within the same family as the prior, facilitating analytical tractability and computational efficiency.
